description:
Roman soldiers had a marching name for Mars. They called him Gradivus, the one who strides forward. Two thousand years later, a human is finally going to stride across Mars itself, and we want to be the team that shows them the way.

If you're eager to do something meaningful, we need you.
summary:
NAVASA (Navigation Assistance System for Aliens) is an offline-first mission planner and tracker that helps astronauts plan and follow a walk on Mars using only NASA data. On Mars, we are the aliens.

Our first mission follows the water in Jezero Crater to the rocks where Perseverance found a potential biosignature. NAVASA layers HiRISE 25 cm images and 1 m terrain, the USGS geologic map, THEMIS thermal data, Perseverance photos and MEDA temperature measurements on one map. For every leg between four stops it calculates two real routes: the shortest (8.9 km, steepest point 31.7°) and the gentlest (10.7 km, steepest 12.8°). It adds a Mars clock with terrain shadows, radio line of sight, Earth light-time delay and a 3D view.

As a mission tracker, it shows the objective, marks stops as reached and points to the next one. It is reusable: a built-in editor creates new missions, and a new Mars site needs only one mission file plus the same kinds of NASA data.

It runs with no internet on a habitat screen, tablet or wrist display. Every number is labelled NASA data or calculated, with its source for the first people to walk on Mars.
details:
What it does
NAVASA (Navigation Assistance System for Aliens) is an offline-first mission planner and tracker for astronauts walking on Mars. Our first mission, “Follow the water to a potential biosignature”, leads through four stops in Jezero Crater: the crater floor, the delta front, Neretva Vallis and Bright Angel, where Perseverance found a potential biosignature.

How it works
A Python pipeline turns NASA data into a data pack once per mission. A plain web app then reads that pack, with no server, and works with Wi-Fi off.

  • MAP: HiRISE 25 cm image, slope, USGS rock units and THEMIS day/night infrared, from a planet view down to the walk area; elevation, slope and rock unit under the cursor; a 3D terrain view.
  • ROUTE: for every leg, two real routes calculated from the HiRISE 1 m terrain model. The shortest walk is 8.9 km with a steepest point of 31.7°; the gentlest is 10.7 km with a steepest point of 12.8°. Each shows distance, climb, descent and where the steepest point is.
  • STOPS: rock unit and description from the geologic map, two real Perseverance photos, the mission question, and “mark stop as reached”.
  • SKY: a Mars clock (sol, local time, sunrise, sunset) using NASA’s Mars24 algorithm; terrain shadows on the routes at any time; radio line of sight between astronauts and the habitat; the light-time delay to Earth.
  • MISSION: objective with sources, progress, next stop with bearing and distance, temperatures Perseverance’s MEDA measured at each stop, an EVA timer, and a mission editor to create, export and import new missions.
  • DATA: the source, date and method of every layer and number.

Benefits

  • One map instead of many separate NASA datasets.
  • Route choices backed by real numbers: walking 1.8 km more makes the worst slope about 19° gentler.
  • Works without internet: on a habitat screen, a tablet or a wrist display.
  • Honest: every value is labelled NASA DATA or CALCULATED, with its source, and the known limits are stated in the app.

Intended impact
Help future crews and mission planners decide where to walk, when and how, using facts rather than guesses. NAVASA is also reusable: a new mission is one file, and a new Mars site needs that file plus the same kinds of NASA data and one command. Because it is free and runs in any browser, students and the public can explore real Mars data too.

Tools and technologies

  • Data processing: Python with NumPy, rasterio, scikit-image, Matplotlib and Pillow; GDAL for a one-time conversion of the geologic map.
  • App: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript; Leaflet for the 2D map; Three.js for the 3D terrain; a Service Worker for offline use.
  • Quality: 124 automated tests, including checks that the browser maths matches the Python pipeline.
  • Delivery: Git, GitHub, GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages.
  • Hardware: none beyond a laptop; the wrist unit is a concept drawn in the browser.

NASA data

  • HiRISE 25 cm image and 1 m terrain (MRO, mosaics by USGS)
  • USGS SIM 3464 geologic map of Jezero
  • THEMIS infrared (Mars Odyssey)
  • Viking colour map of Mars (also via Mars Trek)
  • Perseverance raw images, rover waypoints and MEDA measurements
  • NASA Mars24, JPL planet positions and the NASA Mars Fact Sheet

How it is creative

  • It compares instead of judging: no invented safety limit, just the shortest route next to the gentlest one (the route whose steepest point is as low as possible).
  • Sun, shadows, radio and Earth delay are worked out for the real terrain at the time you choose.
  • The whole mission lives in one file, so new missions need no new code.
  • A terminal-style interface that fits a habitat screen, a tablet and a wrist unit on a spacesuit sleeve.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific facts only: no number without a NASA source or a stated method; missing data is shown as “no data”, never filled in.
  • Offline use: there is no internet on Mars, so detail is saved along the routes.
  • Usability: readable at arm’s length, large touch targets, meaning never shown by colour alone.
  • Security: no server, a strict content security policy, and the map library stored with the app.
  • Honest limits: obstacles smaller than about 1 m are not in the terrain data, and there is no live weather.
  • Time: built solo in 48 hours, with a working core first.
